title: FROM ENEMY TO MISSIONARY
paragraphs: The dust had not yet settled.
The screams were still echoing in memory.
The blood of a murdered believer still stained the conscience of history.
And standing near the center of that darkness was a man named Saul.
Not a criminal hiding in shadows.
Not a pagan king worshiping idols.
A man convinced he was serving God.
That is what makes his story terrifying.
And that is exactly why it gives hope to every soul who wonders if they have gone too far.
Because the greatest missionary in Christian history began as one of Christianity's fiercest enemies.
The story of Saul becoming Paul is not merely a biography.
It is the Gospel in human form.
It is proof that Jesus Christ does not simply improve lives.
The first time many readers encounter Saul, he is standing at the execution of Stephen, the Church's first recorded martyr.
The Greek text calls him Σαῦλος (Saulos).
Stephen died while Saul believed he was doing the right thing.
That reality should stop every reader.
The most dangerous people are not always those who know they are evil.
Often they are people who sincerely believe they are right while resisting the truth of God.
Saul was not fighting against a movement.
He was fighting against Jesus Himself.
The Greek word used is ἐλυμαίνετο (elymaineto).
It carries the image of a wild beast tearing apart its prey.
Yet while Saul pursued the Church, heaven was already pursuing Saul.
Long before we seek Christ, Christ seeks us.
Long before we call His name, He knows ours.
Long before repentance appears in our hearts, mercy is moving toward us.
Then came the road to Damascus.
History changed because one man encountered the risen Christ.
A light brighter than the desert sun exploded around Saul.
"Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting Me?"
Notice what Jesus did not say.
Christ identifies Himself so completely with His people that attacks against believers become attacks against Him.
The Church is not merely an organization.
"I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting."
The Jesus Saul believed was dead was speaking.
The Jesus Saul thought was a false Messiah was alive.
The Jesus Saul rejected was standing before him as Lord.
No one would have questioned such judgment.
No one would have argued against such justice.
The same hands Saul fought against became the hands extended toward him.
The Hebrew Scriptures had foretold this kind of transforming mercy centuries earlier.
The prophet Ezekiel recorded God's promise:
"And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you." (Ezekiel 36:26)
The Hebrew phrase לֵב חָדָשׁ (lev chadash) means "new heart."
God does not merely renovate sinners.
For three days Saul sat blind.
The man who thought he could see clearly finally understood he had been spiritually blind.
Then God sent a disciple named Ananias.
What happened next may be one of the most difficult acts of obedience in Scripture.
God instructed Ananias to go to Saul.
Go visit the man imprisoning Christians.
Go pray for the man hunting believers.
Go welcome the man who terrifies your community.
The Church often struggles with this reality.
We celebrate grace until God extends it to someone we dislike.
We rejoice in forgiveness until forgiveness reaches our enemy.
Yet Christianity has always been a faith where enemies become family.
Ananias entered the room and spoke two astonishing words:
Because once Christ forgives someone, their past no longer has the final word.
The scales fell from Saul's eyes.
The man who once tried to silence the Gospel became one of its loudest voices.
The man who once spread fear now spread hope.
The man who once dragged believers to prison now planted churches across the Roman Empire.
Paul later described his former life:
"Though formerly I was a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent opponent." (1 Timothy 1:13)
Yet he immediately follows that confession with gratitude.
Because Paul understood something many people never grasp.
Your worst chapter does not determine your final chapter.
The Greek word Paul repeatedly uses for grace is χάρις (charis).
Paul knew he could never erase his past.
He could never bring Stephen back.
He could never undo the suffering he caused.
But Christ had done what Paul could not do for himself.
And when God forgives, He does not merely cancel debt.
The greatest evidence of God's forgiveness was not that Paul escaped judgment.
It was that Paul received a mission.
This is where many believers struggle.
They can imagine God forgiving them.
They cannot imagine God using them.
Yet Scripture repeatedly destroys that misconception.
And yet God used every one of them.
"Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more."
The Greek phrase ὑπερεπερίσσευσεν ἡ χάρις (hypereperisseusen hē charis) is explosive.
Grace did not merely match sin.
That truth still terrifies religious pride and comforts repentant sinners.
Some readers know exactly what this feels like.
You have memories you wish you could erase.
Failures that still wake you in the middle of the night.
You read Paul's story and think:
But you struggle to believe He could forgive you.
That lie has been whispering since Eden.
Jesus did not die only for respectable sinners.
The blood of Christ reaches further than your shame.
The resurrection speaks louder than your past.
And the grace of God runs deeper than your worst mistake.
Paul spent the rest of his life proclaiming the very Gospel he once tried to destroy.
Because he never got over grace.
Many Christians lose their wonder because they forget where they came from.
All flowed from amazement that Jesus would save someone like him.
Perhaps that is the greatest lesson in his story.
The miracle was not merely that an enemy became a missionary.
The miracle was that Jesus loved him enough to make it happen.
And that same Jesus is still transforming lives today.
Maybe you are reading this while carrying guilt.
Maybe you are exhausted from pretending everything is fine.
Maybe you feel disqualified from being used by God.
Maybe your past feels louder than God's promises.
Then remember the road to Damascus.
Remember the scales falling from Saul's eyes.
Remember the persecutor becoming a preacher.
Remember the enemy becoming a missionary.
Because if Jesus could transform Saul, your story is not over either.
And perhaps the most dangerous prayer you can pray today is also the simplest:
Be honest. This hit harder than you expected.
Save this and return to it whenever shame tries to convince you that redemption is impossible.
The same voice that stopped Saul on the road is still calling names in the dark.
